subject: Biochemistry
vignette: A 24-year-old woman presents with sudden severe abdominal pain and is found to have a perforated sigmoid colon. Throughout her life she has bruised easily and had thin, translucent skin with visible veins on the chest and abdomen. Her father died at age 36 of an aortic dissection, and her paternal aunt required surgery for a uterine rupture during pregnancy.
question: Which of the following is the most likely underlying defect in this patient?
explanation_correct: This is the vascular type of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, caused by mutations in type III procollagen (COL3A1). Type III collagen (reticulin) predominates in skin, blood vessels, the uterus, and hollow organs, so defective type III collagen produces thin translucent skin, easy bruising, and catastrophic rupture of the aorta, colon, or gravid uterus. The autosomal dominant inheritance and the family history of aortic dissection and uterine rupture support this diagnosis.

explanation_incorrect.A: Type I collagen defects cause osteogenesis imperfecta with fractures, blue sclerae, and dentinogenesis imperfecta rather than hollow organ rupture.
explanation_incorrect.B: Type V collagen mutations cause the classical form of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome with hyperextensible skin and hypermobile joints, but not the vascular and intestinal fragility seen here.
explanation_incorrect.D: Type IV collagen defects cause Alport syndrome with hematuria and sensorineural hearing loss, not vascular or bowel rupture.
explanation_incorrect.E: Fibrillin-1 mutations cause Marfan syndrome with tall stature, arachnodactyly, lens dislocation, and aortic root aneurysm, but not translucent skin or bowel perforation.

educationalObjective: The vascular type of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome results from defective type III procollagen and predisposes to rupture of the aorta, colon, and gravid uterus.
